[ ](images/clipboard-3845085915.png)

## Why Poisson? (1/2)

We often want to know if events independent in time/space. E.g.:

-   Are some people lucky? `r ji("shamrock")`\
-   Do baseball players go on streaks? `r ji("baseball")`\
-   Do cats stick together, or avoid one another? `r ji("tiger")`

Perhaps we can use real data and contrast it to expectations under a
null model and test. What might that distribution look like?

## Why Poisson? (2/2)

::: r-fit-text
Assuming events are independent the Poisson distribution, the Poisson
describes the expected probability of $X$ of events (successes) in a block of time or
space.
:::

## Poisson experiments (1/3)

Random Events in Time or Space

- The number of successes in the experiment can be *counted*
(discrete).

- The *mean number of events* (successes) that occurs during a specific
interval of time (or space) is known.

- Each outcome is **independent**.

- The probability that a success will occur is *proportional to the
size of the interval*.

## Poisson experiments (2/3)

Random Events in Time or Space

::: goal
Example: Number of births per hour in a given hospital
:::

- The number of successes in the experiment can be counted
(discrete). ![](images/clipboard-421996784.png){width="28"}

- The mean number of successes that occurs during a specific
interval of time (or space) is known.
![](images/clipboard-421996784.png){width="28"}

- Each outcome is independent.
![](images/clipboard-421996784.png){width="28"}

- The probability that a success will occur is proportional to the
size of the interval. ![](images/clipboard-421996784.png){width="28"}

## The Poisson distribution (1/)


Formally: a mathematical description of the probability of $X$ successful outcomes when:


1.  the number of attempts, $n$, is high

2. the probability of success for each attempt, $p$, is low and
    determined through a random process

3. the probability of each attempt, $p$, is independent of prior
    success or failure

::: aside
Remember: a discrete probability distribution (can only take values in the range 0,1,2,…
:::

## The Poisson distribution (2/)


The Poisson distribution describes the expected probability of $X$
independent events in time/space.

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.height=4}
x.start <- sample(rep(1:10,rpois(10,1)))
y.start <- sample(rep(1:10,rpois(10,10)),length(x.start))
clumped.dat <- cbind(jitter(rep(x.start,4), amount = .7),jitter(rep(y.start,4), amount = .7))


x.pois <- sample(rep(1:10,rpois(10,10)), nrow(clumped.dat) )
y.pois <- sample(rep(1:10,rpois(10,10)), nrow(clumped.dat) )
pois.dat <- cbind(jitter(x.pois, amount = 1.5),jitter(y.pois, amount = .15))



my.n.col <- floor(sqrt(nrow(clumped.dat)))
overdisp.dat <-jitter(10*cbind(rep(  (1:my.n.col),my.n.col),rep(1:my.n.col,each=my.n.col))/(my.n.col+.3),amount= .5)
par(mfrow = c(1,3),mar = c(16,3,2,1))
plot(clumped.dat,col="#0072B2", main = "Clumped", axes=FALSE, xlab="",ylab="", pch=16, cex =1.2);box()
plot(pois.dat,col="#0072B2", main = "Random", axes=FALSE, xlab="",ylab="", pch=16, cex = 1.2);box()
plot(overdisp.dat,col="#0072B2", main = "Dispersed",axes=FALSE, xlab="",ylab="", pch=16, cex =1.2);box()
```

## The Poisson distribution (4/)

The Poisson distribution describes the expected probability of $X$
independent events in time/space.

```{r}
my.n.col <- floor(sqrt(nrow(clumped.dat)))
overdisp.dat <-jitter(10*cbind(rep(  (1:my.n.col),my.n.col),rep(1:my.n.col,each=my.n.col))/(my.n.col+.3),amount= .5)
par(mfrow = c(1,3),mar = c(16,3,2,1))
plot(clumped.dat,col="#0072B2", main = "Clumped", axes=FALSE, xlab="Contagious disease\noutbreaks",ylab="", pch=16, cex =1.5);box()
plot(pois.dat,col="#0072B2", main = "Random", axes=FALSE, xlab="Number of mutations carried\nby an individual",ylab="", pch=16, cex = 1.5);box()
plot(overdisp.dat,col="#0072B2", main = "Dispersed",axes=FALSE, xlab="Dispersal of territorial\nanimals along an area",ylab="", pch=16, cex =1.5);box()
```

## The Poisson Equation

Assuming events are random and independent, the probability of observing
$X$ events in a block of time or space equals:

$$\Huge{Pr[X] =\frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{X}}{X!}}$$

- $X$: Number of successes

- $P[X]$: probability of occurrence of $X$ successes in one trial

- $\lambda$ (or $\mu$): the expected (mean) number of events in a block.

- $e$ is the base of $ln()$, aka Euler’s number (a constant, `exp(1)` in R).

::: aside
Note: Many people use $\mu$ in place of $\lambda$
:::

## Poisson: Fish Example (3/) `r ji("fish")`

## Steps in Hypothesis Testing

::: columns

::: {.column width="30%"}

- Find expectations (via simulation or via model)

:::

## Option 1: A Lousy Simulation (1/) `r ji("fish")`

We can put `r fish.sum$total_parasites` on `r fish.sum$total_fish` fish many times to generate a null.

1)  Take 225 parasites and:

    randomly place one parasite in one of 238 fish
    
    repeat for each parasite
    
    the same fish can be the target more than once

. . .

2)  At the end, count the number of parasites in each fish

. . .

3)  Repeat this many, many times

## Option 1: A Lousy Simulation (2/) `r ji("fish")`

```{r option1, fig.cap="Note: the observed data does not include X > 6 but they are possible and are thus shown here."}
n.reps <- 1000
sim <-  tibble(x = sample(factor(1:238), size = n.reps  * 225, replace = TRUE),
       replicate = rep(1:n.reps , each = 225)) |> 
  group_by(replicate ,x) |> 
  summarize(num_parasites = n()) |>
  group_by(replicate ,num_parasites) |> 
  summarize(num_fish = n()) 

sim <-  bind_rows(sim |> summarise(num_fish = 238 - sum(num_fish)) |> mutate(num_parasites=0) |> select(replicate, num_parasites, num_fish), ungroup(sim )) |>
  bind_rows(lousy.fish|> mutate(replicate = 0)) |>
  complete(num_parasites,replicate, fill = list(num_fish = 0)) |>
  mutate(data = ifelse(replicate >0 ,"simulated","observed"))

ggplot()+
  geom_jitter(data = sim |> filter(data == "simulated"), 
              aes(x = num_parasites, y= num_fish), 
              color = "#999999", alpha = .5) +
  geom_point(data = sim |> filter(data == "observed"), 
              aes(x = num_parasites, y= num_fish), color = "#C0532B")  +
  annotate(geom = "text", x = c(6,6) , y = c(90,75), size = 6,
           label = c("Observed","Simulation of Null Model"),
           color = c("#C0532B","#999999"), alpha = c(1,1)) +
  ggtitle(label = "Comparing observations to null distribution",
          subtitle = "Are results unexpected under the null?")+
  ylab("Number of fish")+ 
  xlab("Number of parasites")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:9)+
  theme_tufte() +
  bb_theme() +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank())
```

## Option 2: Derived by formula `r ji("fish")`



$P[X]=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^X}{X!}$

$e=2.718282$

$\lambda = \frac{tot.paras}{tot.fish}=225/238$

Let’s try the first row:

$X=0$

$P[0]=\frac{e^{-0.945}\times 0.945^0}{0!}\approx 0.388$

$\text{\# fish expected}=0.388\times 238=92.5$

Repeat for each row...


## Option 2: Derived by formula `r ji("fish")`

```

```

## Proceed with testing?


::: columns

::: column
-   <font color = "black">Find degrees of freedom</font>\
    df = \# categories - 1 - \# params estimated

<font color = "black">Do we meet $\chi^2$ assumptions?</font>\

-   No expected values $< 1$ &\
-   No more than 20% of expected values $< 5$.

If yes, go on. If no, brainstorm.

:::

::: column


```{r}
lousy.fish |>mutate(expect=238*dpois(x=num_parasites, lambda = 0.9453782)) |> kable() |> kable_styling()
fish.sum |> kable()
```


:::
:::


## We do not meet assumptions, now what?

Options:

-   Go on despite this: if test is robust to violations. (I don’t
    support this option!)

-   Combine categories: if biologically sensible.

-   Find a more appropriate test.

-   Bypass traditional tests by using simulations (which we've done)

## We can combine 4+ to meet assumptions

```{r, echo=FALSE}
expecting.fish <- lousy.fish %>% 
  mutate(n = num_parasites * num_fish) %>% 
  mutate(tot.fish = sum(num_fish), 
            tot.parasite = sum(num_parasites * num_fish), 
            mu = tot.parasite / tot.fish  ) %>%
  mutate(expect = tot.fish * dpois(x = num_parasites, lambda = mu))
this.lambda <- with(fish.sum,total_parasites / total_fish )
new.expect <- bind_rows(expecting.fish[1:4,]|> 
  mutate(num_parasites = as.character(num_parasites)) ,
  expecting.fish[-c(1:4),] |> summarise(num_parasites="4+", num_fish = sum(num_fish), n=NA, tot.fish=238, tot.parasite=225, mu=this.lambda, expect=tot.fish*sum(dpois(x = 4:9,lambda = this.lambda))))     
new.expect<-new.expect|> 
  mutate(sq_dev = (expect - num_fish)^2 /expect 	 ) |> mutate(expect = round(expect, digits = 2),sq_dev  = round(sq_dev , digits = 2)) |>  select(-n)
new.expect |> kable() |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

$\chi^ 2= 1.20 + 2.72 + 0.17 + 0.07 + 0.40 =  4.56$

## Hypothesis test

df = \# categories - 1 - \# params estimated = 5 - 1 - 1 = 3

```{r, echo = T}
new.expect |> 
  summarise(chi2 = sum(sq_dev), 
            p_value = pchisq(q = chi2,df =  3, lower.tail = FALSE))                                 
```

## Old fashioned moment

$df=3; \chi^2 = 4.56$
```{r table}
tmp <- bind_cols(df = 1:3,data.frame(t(sapply(1:3, function(X){
  qchisq(p = c(.1,.05,10^(-2:-7)), df = X, lower.tail = FALSE)}
  )))) |> 
  select('df | a' = df, '0.1' = X1, '0.05' = X2, `10^-2` = X3, `10^-3` = X4, `10^-4` = X5 ,  
         `10^-5` = X6,  `10^-6` = X7 ,  `10^-7` = X8)
tmp |>  kable(format = "html", escape = F, digits = 2) |> 
  kable_styling( position = "left") |>
  row_spec(0,  color = "lightgrey", background = "black") |>
  #row_spec(1:12, font_size =  0) |>
  column_spec(2:8, width_min = 10, width_max = 10) 

```

Assuming $\alpha=0.05$, we fail to reject the NULL hypothesis ($P>\alpha$). We cannot exclude the idea that parasites are distributed at random across fish.

# Are counts over or underdispersed {.dark-theme .center}

## Over or underdispersed

- A particular feature of the Poisson distribution is that the variance equals the mean. 

- Sample counts therefore vary more as the mean increases.



If the variance greatly exceeds the mean events are clumped

If the variance is much less than the mean events are dispersed.

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.height=4}
x.start <- sample(rep(1:10,rpois(10,1)))
y.start <- sample(rep(1:10,rpois(10,10)),length(x.start))
clumped.dat <- cbind(jitter(rep(x.start,4), amount = .7),jitter(rep(y.start,4), amount = .7))


x.pois <- sample(rep(1:10,rpois(10,10)), nrow(clumped.dat) )
y.pois <- sample(rep(1:10,rpois(10,10)), nrow(clumped.dat) )
pois.dat <- cbind(jitter(x.pois, amount = 1.5),jitter(y.pois, amount = .15))



my.n.col <- floor(sqrt(nrow(clumped.dat)))
overdisp.dat <-jitter(10*cbind(rep(  (1:my.n.col),my.n.col),rep(1:my.n.col,each=my.n.col))/(my.n.col+.3),amount= .5)
par(mfrow = c(1,3),mar = c(16,3,2,1))
plot(clumped.dat,col="#0072B2", main = expression(Clumped~sigma^2 > lambda), axes=FALSE, xlab="",ylab="", pch=16, cex =1.2);box()
plot(pois.dat,col="#0072B2", main = expression(Random~sigma^2 == lambda), axes=FALSE, xlab="",ylab="", pch=16, cex = 1.2);box()
plot(overdisp.dat,col="#0072B2", main = expression(Dispersed~sigma^2 < lambda),axes=FALSE, xlab="",ylab="", pch=16, cex =1.2);box()
```

## Goodness of fit: Key points (1/)

- A test of $\chi^2$ goodness of fit compares the frequency distribution of a discrete or categorical variable with the frequencies expected from a probability model.
- The test can be applied to many distributions
- More general than the binomial test because it
can handle more than two categories.
- Goodness of fit is measured with the $\chi^2$ test statistic. Its theoretical distribution is continuous. Probability is measured by the area under the curve.
- The $\chi^2$ distribution predicts the deviation of count data from expectations under $H_0$.


## Goodness of fit: Key points (2/)


• Proportional probability model: events fall in
different categories in proportion to the number of
opportunities.
• The Poisson distribution model: describes the
frequency distribution of successes in blocks of
time or space when successes happen
independently and with equal probability over
time or space.
